hero.title: The Complete Guide to AI Reporting Workflows with Claude + MCP
hero.excerpt: Automate data collection, analysis, and reporting with Claude AI and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in a secure, scalable architecture.

intro.text: Manual reporting is slow, repetitive, and error-prone. By combining Claude AI's advanced reasoning capabilities with the ==Model Context Protocol (MCP)==, you can build a powerful reporting workflow that collects data, analyzes it, and generates actionable insights—automatically.

blocks.text: **Claude** is an advanced AI assistant from Anthropic that excels at understanding, analyzing, and generating human-like text.
**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** is an open protocol that allows AI models like Claude to securely connect with external tools, data sources, and systems in a standardized way.
Together, Claude + MCP enable AI to access real-world data, perform complex analysis, and deliver business-ready reports in a consistent, repeatable workflow.

sections.heading: Why Use Claude and MCP for Reporting?

items.title: Save Time
items.text: Automate data gathering and report generation.

items.title: Increase Accuracy
items.text: AI minimizes human error and ensures consistency.

items.title: Deeper Insights
items.text: Claude analyzes data and explains trends clearly.

items.title: Scalable
items.text: Easily handle more data sources and complex reporting needs.

blocks.text: The workflow connects your data sources to Claude through MCP, processes the data, and outputs a well-structured report.

steps.title: Define the Reporting Goal
steps.text: Identify what metrics and insights your report should include.

steps.title: Connect Data Sources via MCP
steps.text: Use MCP connectors to pull data from your databases, APIs, or SaaS tools.

steps.title: Send Data to Claude
steps.text: Pass the retrieved data and reporting instructions to Claude for analysis.

steps.title: Analyze and Generate Insights
steps.text: Claude processes the data, identifies trends, and writes natural-language insights.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: Use Claude prompts that clearly define:
A weekly sales report that used to take an analyst three hours now runs in under a minute.

blocks.code: Prompt: "Using the attached orders export, write a weekly sales summary. Include revenue vs last week, top 5 products, and one risk to watch."

blocks.text: We went from a Monday-morning scramble to a report waiting in the inbox before anyone logged in.

items: Give Claude the smallest dataset that answers the question - not the whole database.
Version your prompts alongside your code.
Always keep a human review step before a report is shared externally.
Log every run so you can trace how a number was produced.

blocks.title: Watch your data scope
blocks.text: Only expose the MCP resources a workflow actually needs. Broad read access is the most common security mistake.

rows: Google Sheets, Postgres, Shopify Admin API
Official reference servers, custom Node/Python server

items.title: Hallucinated numbers
items.text: Feed structured data and ask Claude to cite the row it used.

items.title: Large datasets

items.title: Stale data

items.title: Inconsistent format

seo.title: Speeding Up Your Shopify Store: A Practical Checklist | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A field-tested checklist for improving Shopify load times, from image handling and app audits to theme code and Core Web Vitals.

hero.title: Speeding Up Your Shopify Store: A Practical Checklist
hero.excerpt: A field-tested checklist for improving Shopify load times, from image handling and app audits to theme code and Core Web Vitals.

intro.text: Speed is a conversion feature. A one-second delay on mobile can measurably drop add-to-cart rate. This is the checklist we run on every ==Shopify performance audit==, in the order we run it.

blocks.text: You cannot improve what you have not measured. Get a baseline on a **real device on 4G**, not just a desktop lab score.

items: Run PageSpeed Insights on the home page, a collection, and a product page.
Record Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
Check the field data section - that is what Google actually ranks on.

blocks.title: Target numbers
blocks.text: LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1 - measured on mobile field data, not lab.

sections.heading: Fix Images First - It Is Usually the Biggest Win

items.title: Serve modern formats
items.text: Shopify auto-serves WebP - make sure your theme uses the image_url filter, not hardcoded src.

items.title: Right-size
items.text: Never ship a 3000px hero to a 400px phone. Use responsive srcset with width descriptors.

items.title: Lazy-load below the fold
items.text: loading="lazy" on everything except the LCP image.

items.title: Reserve space
items.text: Always set width and height so the layout does not jump (CLS).

blocks.text: Every app can inject JavaScript into every page. The average store carries 3-6 apps it no longer uses.

rows: Keep if it earns its keep in revenue

blocks.title: Uninstalling is not enough
blocks.text: Many apps leave Liquid snippets and script tags behind. Search your theme for the app name after removing it.

steps.title: Defer non-critical JavaScript
steps.text: Add defer to script tags that are not needed for first paint.

steps.title: Preload the LCP image and fonts
steps.text: One rel=preload for the hero image and your primary web font.

steps.title: Remove unused CSS
steps.text: Old sections and settings often leave dead styles in theme.css.

steps.title: Cut render-blocking third parties
steps.text: Load chat widgets and analytics after the page is interactive.

blocks.text: Re-run the same three pages on the same device. Then add a monthly recurring check so regressions from new apps or campaigns get caught early.
We cut LCP from 4.1s to 2.0s on mobile and add-to-cart rate went up 9% the same month.

items.q: Does a higher PageSpeed score guarantee more sales?
items.a: No. It removes a barrier. Speed helps most when your store is currently slow on mobile; going from 90 to 95 rarely moves revenue.

items.q: Should I switch themes for speed?
items.a: Only if your current theme is an old vintage (non-OS 2.0) build. A modern theme plus this checklist usually beats a rushed migration.

items.q: Are page builders always slow?
items.a: Not always, but they add weight. Use them for landing pages, not your core product template.

seo.title: The Checkout Friction Audit: Find What Is Costing You Sales | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A structured way to walk your own checkout, score every point of friction, and prioritise the fixes that recover the most revenue.

hero.title: The Checkout Friction Audit: Find What Is Costing You Sales
hero.excerpt: A structured way to walk your own checkout, score every point of friction, and prioritise the fixes that recover the most revenue.

intro.text: Most stores obsess over traffic and ignore the last 30 seconds of the journey. A ==checkout friction audit== is the cheapest CRO work you can do: no tools, no budget, just one focused hour walking your own funnel like a first-time buyer.

blocks.text: Friction compounds. A tiny hesitation at each step adds up to a closed tab. Write down every screen between product and confirmation.

sections.heading: Walk It on a Phone, on Data

steps.title: Use a real phone on cellular
steps.text: Not desktop, not wifi. Most abandonment happens on mobile data.

steps.title: Buy something for real
steps.text: Go all the way to a completed order. Refund it after.

steps.title: Narrate out loud
steps.text: Every time you pause, squint, or reach for information you do not have - that is friction. Note it.

steps.title: Repeat as a guest
steps.text: No saved address, no autofill. That is your hardest-working new customer.

blocks.text: If you hesitate for even half a second, a real customer hesitates longer - and some of them leave. Every pause is a line item.
Rate every issue you found on impact and effort, then sort. Fix high-impact / low-effort first.

rows: No express payment (Shop Pay / Apple Pay)
Surprise shipping cost at final step

sections.heading: The Fixes That Show Up Every Time

items.title: Enable express checkout
items.text: Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay above the fold in cart and checkout.

items.title: Show shipping early
items.text: Estimate cost and date in the cart, before the customer commits.

items.title: Guest checkout default
items.text: Offer an account after purchase, never before.

items.title: Trust near payment
items.text: Return policy, secure-payment note, and support contact by the pay button.

blocks.title: Do not fix everything at once
blocks.text: Ship changes in small batches so you can tell which one moved the number.
Track cart-to-checkout and checkout-to-purchase rates weekly. A friction audit that does not change those numbers was a list, not a fix.
Removing forced signup and adding Shop Pay took an afternoon and lifted checkout completion by 11%.

items.q: How often should I run this?
items.a: Once a quarter, and always after a theme update, a new checkout app, or a payment provider change.

items.q: Shopify checkout is locked down - what can I actually change?
items.a: Plenty: express payments, cart page UX, shipping presentation, trust content, and (on Plus) checkout extensions.

items.q: Do I need session recording tools?
items.a: They help, but the manual walk-through finds most issues for free. Add tools once you have exhausted the obvious.

seo.title: Reading A/B Test Results Without Fooling Yourself | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: The statistical traps that make losing tests look like winners, and a simple discipline for calling results you can trust.

hero.title: Reading A/B Test Results Without Fooling Yourself
hero.excerpt: The statistical traps that make losing tests look like winners, and a simple discipline for calling results you can trust.

intro.text: The hardest part of A/B testing is not running the test - it is not lying to yourself about the result. ==Peeking, tiny samples, and ignored guardrail metrics== turn noise into false confidence, and false confidence ships changes that quietly cost money.

sections.heading: "95% Significant" Is Not a Finish Line

blocks.text: Statistical significance tells you the result is unlikely to be pure chance *given the data so far*. It says nothing about whether you collected enough data, or whether you looked too early.

blocks.title: Peeking inflates false positives
blocks.text: If you check the dashboard daily and stop the moment it hits 95%, your real false-positive rate is closer to 25-30%, not 5%.

sections.heading: Decide the Rules Before You Launch

items: Pick the primary metric. One. Everything else is a guardrail or secondary.
Estimate the minimum detectable effect you would care about.
Use a sample-size calculator to get the required visitors per variant.
Convert that to a duration in whole business weeks, and commit to it.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: Write these four numbers in the test ticket before it goes live:
A variant can lift clicks and wreck revenue. Always read the whole picture.

rows: New friction later in the funnel
Segment before you roll out to everyone

blocks.text: A 50/50 test that delivered 54/46 has a **sample ratio mismatch**. Something is broken - a redirect, a bot filter, an analytics gap - and the result is not trustworthy, however pretty the graph.

blocks.title: Quick gut check
blocks.text: With tens of thousands of visitors, a genuine 50/50 split stays within roughly a percentage point. Bigger gaps need investigation, not interpretation.

items.title: Ship it
items.text: Hit the pre-planned sample, significant on primary, guardrails clean.

items.title: Re-run it
items.text: Promising but under-powered, or a data issue mid-flight.

items.title: Kill it
items.text: Flat or negative at full sample. A clean null is a real, useful result.

items.title: Segment then decide
items.text: Strong on one device or audience, neutral elsewhere.

blocks.text: Half our "winners" stopped winning once we forced ourselves to wait for the planned sample size.

items.q: Can I ever stop a test early?
items.a: Only to stop a clearly harmful variant, or if the tool uses a sequential/Bayesian method designed for continuous monitoring. Not to lock in a win.

items.q: What if the test never reaches significance?
items.a: That is an answer: the effect is smaller than you hoped. Ship the cheaper variant or move on.

items.q: How many tests should be winners?
items.a: Industry-wide, roughly 1 in 5 to 1 in 8. If most of your tests win, your analysis is too loose.

seo.title: Building a Pre-Launch QA Process That Scales | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: How to turn ad-hoc launch-day panic into a repeatable QA process: environments, a tiered checklist, automation, and a go/no-go gate.

hero.title: Building a Pre-Launch QA Process That Scales
hero.excerpt: How to turn ad-hoc launch-day panic into a repeatable QA process: environments, a tiered checklist, automation, and a go/no-go gate.

intro.text: Every store has a QA process. For most it is called "the founder clicks around for ten minutes and hopes." That works until it does not - usually on the highest-traffic day of the year. A ==repeatable QA process== is boring on purpose, and it scales with your release cadence.

sections.heading: Test Somewhere That Looks Like Production

blocks.text: Bugs hide in the gap between your test setup and the real store. Close that gap first.

items: Use a duplicate theme or a dedicated staging store, not the live theme's edit mode.
Seed realistic data: real product counts, real collection sizes, a discount code, an out-of-stock variant.
Test with production-like apps installed - app conflicts are a top launch-day failure.

blocks.title: Keep a throwaway order path
blocks.text: A $0.01 hidden product plus a 100%-off code lets you complete real checkouts without touching payouts.

sections.heading: A Checklist With Tiers, Not 200 Flat Items

blocks.text: Nobody runs a 200-line checklist honestly. Split it by risk so the right depth matches the change.

items.title: Smoke (every deploy)
items.text: Home, collection, product, cart, checkout complete. 5 minutes.

items.title: Core (weekly release)
items.text: Search, filters, account, discounts, email receipts, key landing pages.

items.title: Cross-device (theme change)
items.text: iOS Safari, Android Chrome, one small viewport, one desktop.

items.title: Full regression (big launch)
items.text: Everything, plus load test and analytics/pixel verification.

steps.title: Pick the tier
steps.text: Match it to the size of the change, decided by the person merging.

steps.title: Run it on staging
steps.text: Log every failure with a screenshot, URL, device, and steps to reproduce.

steps.title: Triage
steps.text: Blocker, major, or minor. Blockers stop the release; minors get tickets.

steps.title: Re-test fixes only
steps.text: Verify each fix and one thing around it - not the whole checklist again.

blocks.label: PRO TIP
blocks.text: A good bug report has all of these - missing one wastes a round-trip:
You will never automate everything, and you should not try. Automate the checks that are identical every time and expensive to miss.

rows: Highest cost of failure, stable steps
Visual layout of a campaign page
Changes constantly, human eye is faster
Silent when broken, big blind spot

blocks.text: One named person makes the call, against written criteria, and records it. That is the whole ritual - it just has to happen every time.

blocks.title: Ship criteria
blocks.text: Zero open blockers, smoke suite green on staging and production, rollback plan written, owner on call for two hours after launch.

blocks.alt: A team reviewing a launch checklist on a screen
blocks.caption: The gate is a five-minute conversation, not a committee.

items.q: We are a team of two. Is this overkill?
items.a: Scale it down: just the smoke tier and a one-line go/no-go. The structure matters more than the size.

items.q: What should we automate first?
items.a: The checkout-complete path. It has the highest cost of failure and the most stable steps.

items.q: How do we stop the checklist rotting?
items.a: Review it after every incident. If a bug reached production, add or change one line so it cannot happen silently again.

seo.title: Designing Product Pages That Sell | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: A design-led breakdown of the product page: hierarchy, imagery, the buy box, proof, and the details that quietly decide the sale.

hero.title: Designing Product Pages That Sell
hero.excerpt: A design-led breakdown of the product page: hierarchy, imagery, the buy box, proof, and the details that quietly decide the sale.

intro.text: The product page is where browsing becomes buying. Good PDP design is not decoration - it is ==answering the customer's questions in the order they ask them==, and removing every reason to hesitate before the add-to-cart tap.

blocks.text: On mobile the customer sees one screen at a time. Decide what each screen has to accomplish before you choose a single colour or font.
If a first-time visitor cannot tell what the product is, what it costs, and how to buy it within one thumb-scroll, the design has failed - regardless of how it looks.

items.title: Show scale
items.text: The product in a hand, on a body, in a room. Absolute size is invisible without context.

items.title: Show the range
items.text: Every colourway and key angle. Missing an angle reads as hiding something.

items.title: Show detail
items.text: One tight crop of texture, stitching, or finish quality.

items.title: Design for the phone
items.text: First image must read at 375px wide. Test it there, not on your monitor.

sections.heading: The Buy Box Is Sacred Space

blocks.text: Price, variant selection, quantity, and the add-to-cart button. Nothing competes with these. Every extra element here is a tax on the conversion.

items: Selected variant is always obvious - a state, not a guess.
Unavailable combinations are visibly disabled, not silently broken.
The button says what happens next ("Add to cart"), never just "Submit".
Shipping estimate and return terms sit one line below, not three taps away.

blocks.title: Sticky bars help - until they cover content
blocks.text: A sticky add-to-cart on mobile lifts conversion, but make sure it never hides the variant picker or size guide.

steps.title: Rating near the title
steps.text: A star rating by the product name answers "is this any good?" instantly.

steps.title: Reviews after the description
steps.text: Once they know what it is, they want to know if it delivered.

steps.title: Photos from customers
steps.text: Real-world images beat studio shots for believability.

steps.title: Objection-handling FAQ last
steps.text: Fit, care, compatibility, delivery - the questions that stall a purchase.

blocks.text: We moved the review stars up next to the title and nothing else. PDP conversion rose about 6%.

sections.heading: The Details That Quietly Decide It

rows: Size guide in a modal, not a new page
Keeps the customer in the flow
Fake urgency is detected and punished

blocks.title: The test
blocks.text: Read your PDP as someone about to spend their own money on a brand they have never heard of. Every unanswered question is a lost sale.

items.q: How long should the description be?
items.a: Short value copy high up, full detail lower down. Let confident buyers add to cart in seconds and researchers keep scrolling.

items.q: Video or photos?
items.a: Photos are non-negotiable. Video is a strong addition for products where motion, fit, or use is hard to convey in a still.

items.q: Should every product page look identical?
items.a: The structure should. The content depth can flex - a $15 accessory needs far less page than a $400 mattress.

seo.title: Collection Page Design: Helping Shoppers Find the Right Product Fast | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: How to design collection pages that shorten the path from browsing to the right product: layout, filters, product cards, and sorting.

hero.title: Collection Page Design: Helping Shoppers Find the Right Product Fast
hero.excerpt: How to design collection pages that shorten the path from browsing to the right product: layout, filters, product cards, and sorting.

intro.text: Everyone designs the product page. Almost nobody designs the collection page on purpose, and yet it is where most shoppers decide which product deserves a click. A good collection page is not a catalogue. It is ==a sorting machine== that gets a shopper from 'I need something like this' to 'this one' in as few steps as possible.

blocks.text: Every collection page answers a question. 'Show me running shoes' is broad; 'show me waterproof trail shoes under a budget' is specific. Your layout should make both questions easy. Before touching the design, list the **three to five attributes** customers actually use to choose inside this collection: size, price, use case, material, colour.
Check your site search and support tickets. The words customers type are the filters they want.

The product card is the smallest unit of the page and it is repeated dozens of times, so small decisions compound. Each card should answer: what is it, how much is it, and why this one over its neighbour.

steps.title: Image that shows the product clearly
steps.text: Consistent crop, consistent background. Use a hover or second image for context, not a different angle of the same shot.

steps.title: Title that differentiates
steps.text: 'Trail Runner GTX - Waterproof' beats 'Trail Runner'. Put the deciding attribute in the name.

steps.title: Price with honest discounts
steps.text: Show compare-at pricing only when it is real. Fake discounts erode trust fast.

steps.title: One proof signal
steps.text: A star rating or 'bestseller' badge. Not both plus three more badges.

sections.heading: Filters That Help Instead of Overwhelm

blocks.text: Filters are where collection pages win or lose. Too few and shoppers scroll endlessly; too many and they freeze.

rows: No visible count of active filters

blocks.title: No dead ends
blocks.text: Always show how many products match each filter, and never let a filter combination return zero results without offering a way back.

sections.heading: Sort Order Is a Merchandising Decision

blocks.text: The default sort is the most-viewed layout on your site, and most stores leave it on 'Featured' with no one owning what 'featured' means. Decide it deliberately: **bestsellers first** for conversion, **new arrivals first** for repeat-visit brands, or a **manual order** that balances margin and stock.

items: Push out-of-stock items to the end, or hide them.
Keep the first row strong: it sets expectations for the whole collection.
Review default sort monthly, not yearly.

blocks.text: On a phone, a two-column grid is usually right. One column feels slow, three is unreadable. Keep the filter button sticky so shoppers can refine without scrolling back up, and make sure the active filter count is visible at all times.

blocks.title: The metric to watch
blocks.text: Measure collection-to-product click-through rate. If it drops on mobile compared with desktop, the layout is the first suspect.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [Designing Product Pages That Sell](/designing-product-pages-that-sell)
[Mobile CRO: Designing for Small Screens](/mobile-cro-designing-small-screens)

items.q: Should I use infinite scroll or pagination?
items.a: Load-more buttons are usually the best compromise: shoppers keep their place, and the footer stays reachable.

items.q: How many products should a collection show above the fold?
items.a: On mobile, aim for at least two full product cards visible without scrolling past banners.

items.q: Do collection banners help?
items.a: Only if they add information. A large lifestyle image that pushes products below the fold usually costs clicks.

seo.title: Homepage Design for E-commerce: What Actually Earns the Scroll | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Your homepage is a routing page, not a brochure. A section-by-section guide to homepage design that moves visitors into the store.

hero.title: Homepage Design for E-commerce: What Actually Earns the Scroll
hero.excerpt: Your homepage is a routing page, not a brochure. A section-by-section guide to homepage design that moves visitors into the store.

intro.text: Founders spend weeks on the homepage, then discover in analytics that most sales start somewhere else. That is not a reason to ignore it. It is a reason to design it for its real job: ==getting new visitors to the right product quickly== and telling them, in seconds, why this brand is worth their time.

sections.heading: Know What the Homepage Is For

blocks.text: Look at where homepage visitors go next. In most stores, the top exits from the homepage are the main navigation, a hero button, and one or two featured collections. That tells you the homepage is a **routing page**. Design it like one.
Pull the 'next page' report for your homepage before redesigning. It shows what visitors actually want from it.

sections.heading: The Hero: One Message, One Action

blocks.text: The hero section has one job: say what you sell and who it is for, then give a clear path in. Rotating sliders dilute that. By the second slide, most visitors have already scrolled or clicked away.

steps.title: Headline that states the offer
steps.text: Clear beats clever. 'Organic skincare for sensitive skin' says more than 'Glow differently'.

steps.title: Supporting line with a reason to care
steps.text: Free shipping, a guarantee, a key benefit: one line.

steps.title: One primary button
steps.text: Point it at your best-converting collection, not a generic 'Shop all'.

steps.title: Image that shows the product in use
steps.text: Lifestyle is fine if the product is still recognisable.

sections.heading: Build the Scroll in Order of Intent

rows: Route browsers to the right collection
It converts better than the collection page
Capture visitors not ready to buy
It offers a clear reason to join

blocks.title: Decoration has a cost
blocks.text: Anything that does not route, reassure, or capture is decoration. Decoration is fine only when it does not push useful sections further down.

A returning customer does not need your brand story again. Consider surfacing 'recently viewed' or new arrivals higher for known visitors. Even without full personalisation, a **'New this week'** row gives regulars a reason to scroll.

items: Track clicks per section, not just overall bounce rate.
Use scroll-depth data to see where attention drops off.
Remove or move sections that get attention but no clicks.

blocks.title: The rule of thumb
blocks.text: A shorter homepage that routes well usually beats a longer one that tries to say everything.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [Data-Driven Redesigns](/data-driven-redesigns)
[The Role of Social Proof in CRO](/role-of-social-proof-in-cro)

items.q: Are sliders always bad?
items.a: Not always, but auto-rotating sliders rarely outperform a single strong hero. If you use one, test it against a static version.

items.q: Should the homepage show prices?
items.a: Yes, in any product rows. Price is part of the decision and hiding it adds a click.

items.q: How often should I update the homepage?
items.a: Refresh product rows with each campaign or season; revisit the structure quarterly using click data.

seo.title: Post-Purchase Upsells: The Revenue Most Stores Leave on the Table | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: The moment after checkout is the most trusted moment in the journey. Here is how to use post-purchase offers without hurting the experience.

hero.title: Post-Purchase Upsells: The Revenue Most Stores Leave on the Table
hero.excerpt: The moment after checkout is the most trusted moment in the journey. Here is how to use post-purchase offers without hurting the experience.

intro.text: Most CRO work focuses on getting the first order. But the seconds right after a purchase are unusually valuable: the customer has just trusted you with their card, the payment details are known, and the hesitation that slows every other step is gone. A well-built post-purchase offer turns that goodwill into ==extra revenue without adding friction== to the original checkout.

blocks.text: A pre-purchase upsell competes with the main sale. If the customer hesitates, you risk the whole order. A post-purchase offer comes **after the order is already secured**, so the downside is small: the worst case is a customer who says no and still has their original order.
Post-purchase offers add revenue without risking the conversion you already earned. That is why they are often a low-risk first test for AOV.

rows: Case for a phone, refill for a bottle
Add a second pack at a lower unit price
Your top seller at a one-time discount
Convert this order into a subscription

blocks.text: The offer should feel like a natural next step, not a random promotion. **Relevance matters more than the size of the discount.**

steps.title: Confirm the order first
steps.text: Say clearly that their order is placed. Anxiety kills the upsell.

steps.title: One offer at a time
steps.text: A single product with one image, one price, one button.

steps.title: One-click accept
steps.text: No re-entering payment details. That is the whole advantage.

steps.title: An obvious decline
steps.text: 'No thanks, view my order' should be easy to find. Hiding it damages trust.

blocks.text: Post-purchase is a window, not a single screen. The order confirmation email, the shipping notification, and the delivery follow-up are all moments of high attention.

items: Add a 'complete the set' block to the confirmation email.
Use the delivery email to ask for a review, then suggest a related product.
Time replenishment reminders to the product's actual usage cycle.

blocks.text: Track **take rate** (how many accept), **revenue per order** including upsells, and **refund rate** on upsold items. A high take rate with high refunds means the offer is too pushy or poorly matched.

blocks.title: One change per test
blocks.text: Test one variable at a time: product, then price, then copy. Changing all three together tells you nothing.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [Shopify Bundles: Boosting AOV](/shopify-bundles-boost-aov)

items.q: Do post-purchase upsells work on standard Shopify?
items.a: Post-purchase pages are supported through apps built on Shopify's post-purchase extensions; check current plan requirements for your store before choosing an app.

items.q: What discount should I offer?
items.a: Start modest. Relevance usually matters more than the size of the discount; test before going deeper.

items.q: Will this annoy customers?
items.a: Not if the order is clearly confirmed, the offer is relevant, and declining takes one click.

seo.title: Site Search Optimization: Turning Searchers Into Buyers | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Visitors who use site search tell you exactly what they want. Here is how to make sure your search results actually deliver it.

hero.title: Site Search Optimization: Turning Searchers Into Buyers
hero.excerpt: Visitors who use site search tell you exactly what they want. Here is how to make sure your search results actually deliver it.

intro.text: A visitor who types into your search bar is doing you a favour: they are telling you ==exactly what they want to buy==. Searchers often convert better than browsers for that reason. Yet on most stores, search is left on default settings and nobody ever checks what happens after someone hits enter.

blocks.text: Start with your search report. Export the top search terms and look at three things: which terms get the most volume, which return zero results, and which have high searches but low conversions.

rows: Leave it, but feature it in navigation
Results are irrelevant or poorly ordered

blocks.text: A blank results page is a dead end. Even when you truly do not stock what they asked for, you can still help.

steps.title: Map synonyms
steps.text: 'Sofa' and 'couch', 'hoodie' and 'sweatshirt'. Your customers do not use your catalogue language.

steps.title: Suggest alternatives
steps.text: Show bestsellers or related categories instead of 'No results found'.

steps.title: Redirect intent queries
steps.text: Searches like 'returns' or 'shipping' should land on the right help page.

steps.title: Log what you cannot fix
steps.text: Repeated zero-result terms are product ideas.

sections.heading: Make the Search Bar Easy to Use

items: On mobile, show a visible search field or a clear icon, not a hidden menu item.
Add predictive search with product images and prices as the shopper types.
Keep the search query visible on the results page so it can be edited.
Allow filtering and sorting inside search results, the same as collections.

blocks.text: Type your own top 20 search terms on a phone this week. You will find at least one surprise.

Default relevance does not know your margins, stock, or bestsellers. For your highest-volume terms, make sure **the first row of results contains products people actually buy**. Many search apps allow pinning or boosting; use them for the terms that matter most.

sections.heading: Track Search as Its Own Funnel

blocks.text: Measure search usage rate, search exit rate, and conversion rate for sessions with search versus without. Review zero-result terms monthly.

blocks.title: Small, steady wins
blocks.text: Search improves quietly, one fixed term at a time.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [Shopify SEO Technical Checklist](/shopify-technical-seo-checklist)
[The Checkout Friction Audit](/checkout-friction-audit-cro)

items.q: Is Shopify's native search good enough?
items.a: For small catalogues, often yes, especially with synonyms configured. Larger catalogues usually benefit from a dedicated search app.

items.q: Should the search bar be expanded by default?
items.a: On stores where search usage is high, a visible search field usually outperforms a hidden icon. Test it.

items.q: How often should I review search data?
items.a: Monthly for top terms and zero-result queries, plus after any catalogue change.

seo.title: Building an A/B Testing Roadmap That Does Not Run Out of Ideas | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: How to source test ideas from real data, prioritise them with a simple scoring model, and keep a testing programme running month after month.

hero.title: Building an A/B Testing Roadmap That Does Not Run Out of Ideas
hero.excerpt: How to source test ideas from real data, prioritise them with a simple scoring model, and keep a testing programme running month after month.

intro.text: Most testing programmes die the same way. The first few tests are obvious, then the team runs out of ideas and starts testing button colours. A testing roadmap fixes that: ==a steady pipeline of evidence-based ideas==, ranked so the highest-value tests always run first.

sections.heading: Source Ideas From Evidence, Not Opinion

blocks.text: Good test ideas come from places where customers are telling you something is wrong. Build your backlog from these sources, not from the last meeting.

rows: What they ignore, misclick, or struggle with
Questions the site fails to answer
What people want but cannot find

sections.heading: Write Every Idea as a Hypothesis

blocks.text: An idea is not ready until it has a reason and a prediction. Use one simple template for every entry in the backlog:
Because we saw **[evidence]**, we believe **[change]** will cause **[outcome]** for **[audience]**. We will know by measuring **[metric]**.
This forces the team to connect each test to data, and makes results easier to learn from, win or lose.
A simple scoring model keeps prioritisation honest. **ICE** is a good starting point: score each idea from 1 to 10 on Impact, Confidence, and Ease, then average.

rows: Add size guide to product page

blocks.title: Read the scores, not just the total
blocks.text: Notice the button colour test scores high on ease alone. Scoring helps expose ideas that are easy but pointless.

Before a test enters the roadmap, estimate whether the page gets enough traffic to detect the effect you expect in a reasonable time. **Low-traffic pages need bigger, bolder changes**, or should be tested with qualitative methods instead.

steps.title: Review the backlog weekly
steps.text: Add new evidence, re-score, retire stale ideas.

steps.title: Document every result
steps.text: Hypothesis, screenshots, numbers, and what you learned.

steps.title: Turn results into new ideas
steps.text: A win on one page often suggests a test on another.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [How Long Should You Run an A/B Test?](/how-long-to-run-ab-test)
[Reading A/B Test Results Without Fooling Yourself](/reading-ab-test-results-without-fooling-yourself)

items.q: How many tests should we run at once?
items.a: As many as your traffic supports without overlapping on the same page and audience. For most stores that is one to three.

items.q: Is ICE better than PIE?
items.a: Both work. The model matters less than scoring consistently and revisiting scores with new data.

items.q: What if a test is inconclusive?
items.a: Record it. An inconclusive result still tells you the change was not a large lever.

seo.title: Testing Prices and Offers Without Burning Customer Trust | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Price and offer tests can move revenue more than any design change, and they can backfire. A careful approach to testing what you charge.

hero.title: Testing Prices and Offers Without Burning Customer Trust
hero.excerpt: Price and offer tests can move revenue more than any design change, and they can backfire. A careful approach to testing what you charge.

intro.text: Few changes move revenue as much as price, and few tests carry as much risk. Show two customers different prices for the same product and one of them may notice, screenshot it, and ask why. Price testing can be done well, but it ==needs more care than testing a headline==.

sections.heading: Decide What You Are Really Testing

blocks.text: 'Price testing' covers several different experiments, and they carry very different levels of risk.

rows: Free shipping at one threshold vs another
Testing a price before it has history
Live price split on existing product
Same item at two prices simultaneously

blocks.text: Start with offer framing and thresholds. They are easier to run and less likely to upset anyone.

A lower price almost always lifts conversion rate. That does not mean it made you more money. For any price or offer test, the primary metric should be **revenue or gross profit per visitor**, not conversion rate alone.

items: Include discount cost and shipping cost in the calculation.
Watch average order value alongside conversion rate.
Where possible, follow cohorts to see whether repeat purchase changes.

steps.title: Test sequentially on new products
steps.text: Launch at one price for a period, then another. Less rigorous, far less risky.

steps.title: Test by market
steps.text: Different regions can carry different prices when that is standard in your category.

steps.title: Test the offer, not the price
steps.text: Keep the list price stable and vary the promotion, bundle, or threshold.

steps.title: Honour the lower price
steps.text: If a customer finds a lower test price, give it to them. A goodwill policy prevents most complaints.

sections.heading: Check the Legal and Platform Side

blocks.text: Rules on price display, reference prices, and discount claims vary by country. Before running any live price split, check the consumer protection rules in the markets you sell to and the terms of your testing tool and platform.

blocks.title: Live price splits need a check first
blocks.text: If in doubt, get advice before you launch.

sections.heading: Run It Longer Than a Design Test

blocks.text: Price affects behaviour over time. Some shoppers compare, leave, and come back. Run price and offer tests across **at least two full weekly cycles**, and avoid overlapping with sales events that distort normal buying.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [How to Calculate Statistical Significance](/calculate-statistical-significance)

items.q: Can I split-test prices on Shopify?
items.a: Some third-party apps support it. Understand how they display prices across the storefront, cart, and checkout before you rely on one.

items.q: Is showing different prices to different people legal?
items.a: It depends on your market and how it is done. Check local consumer protection rules and get advice for live price splits.

items.q: What is the safest first price test?
items.a: Free-shipping threshold tests: low risk, easy to explain, and usually a meaningful lever for AOV.

cta.text: We design offer and pricing experiments that protect both margin and trust.

seo.title: Shopify Metafields and Metaobjects: Custom Content Without Extra Apps | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Use metafields and metaobjects to add size guides, specs, ingredients, and reusable content blocks to your theme without paying for another app.

hero.title: Shopify Metafields and Metaobjects: Custom Content Without Extra Apps
hero.excerpt: Use metafields and metaobjects to add size guides, specs, ingredients, and reusable content blocks to your theme without paying for another app.

intro.text: Many Shopify stores install an app every time they need a new piece of content on a product page: a size chart app, a specs table app, an ingredients app. Each one adds scripts, cost, and another thing to maintain. Metafields and metaobjects let you ==store that content natively and render it in your theme==, often with no app at all.

sections.heading: Metafields vs Metaobjects in Plain Terms

rows: An extra field attached to a product, variant, collection, etc.
A reusable content entry with its own fields
Data unique to one item: material, care notes, weight
Content shared across items: size guides, designers, ingredients
One 'Tops size guide' linked to 200 products

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: if you would copy and paste the same content into many products, it should be a metaobject.

sections.heading: Plan the Data Before You Build

steps.title: List the content that varies
steps.text: Walk through ten product pages and note every piece of content that changes between them.

steps.title: Decide the owner
steps.text: Product-level, variant-level, or shared? This decides metafield vs metaobject.

steps.title: Pick the right field type
steps.text: Use typed fields (number, list, reference, rich text), not plain text for everything.

steps.title: Name it for the team
steps.text: Clear names and descriptions so the merchandising team knows what to fill in.

blocks.text: In Online Store 2.0 themes, many metafields can be connected to theme blocks through **dynamic sources** in the theme editor, with no code. For more control, output them in Liquid inside a snippet or section, and always check the value exists before rendering so empty products do not show broken blocks.

items: Wrap output in a conditional so blank fields show nothing.
Keep formatting in the theme, not in the data.
Build one reusable section per content type, not one per product.

items.title: Size guides
items.text: Linked from product pages as a single metaobject per category.

items.title: Specification tables
items.text: Built from typed fields, consistent across the catalogue.

items.title: Ingredient libraries
items.text: Material or ingredient entries that update everywhere when edited once.

items.title: Collection copy
items.text: Intro copy and FAQs for SEO without theme edits per page.

blocks.text: If you are replacing an app, export its data first and plan the import.

blocks.title: Uninstalling is only half the job
blocks.text: Remove the old app's code snippets from the theme after uninstalling, and QA a sample of products on mobile and desktop before going live.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [Shopify Apps You Can Safely Uninstall](/shopify-apps-safe-to-uninstall)
[Advanced Liquid Snippets](/advanced-liquid-snippets-dynamic-pricing)

items.q: Do metafields slow down my store?
items.a: Metafields rendered in Liquid are part of the page itself, so they usually add far less weight than an app that injects scripts.

items.q: Can non-developers edit metafield content?
items.a: Yes. Once definitions are set up, content is edited in the Shopify admin like any other product field.

items.q: Can I bulk-edit metafields?
items.a: Yes, through the bulk editor or CSV-based tools, which is useful for large catalogues.

seo.title: Selling Internationally on Shopify: A Technical Guide to Markets | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Currencies, domains, languages, duties, and SEO: the technical decisions behind taking a Shopify store international without breaking it.

hero.title: Selling Internationally on Shopify: A Technical Guide to Markets
hero.excerpt: Currencies, domains, languages, duties, and SEO: the technical decisions behind taking a Shopify store international without breaking it.

intro.text: Going international used to mean cloning your store for every country. Shopify Markets changed that, letting one store serve multiple regions. But 'turn it on' is not a strategy. The decisions you make about ==domains, currency, language, and pricing== shape conversion, SEO, and operations for years.

sections.heading: Start With the Market, Not the Settings

blocks.text: Before configuring anything, look at where your international traffic and orders already come from. Pick **one or two markets** where demand exists, then build properly for those rather than switching on every country at once.
Your analytics already show which countries want to buy. Start there.

rows: Simplest; keeps SEO authority on one domain
Strong local signal; more to manage

blocks.title: Verify hreflang
blocks.text: Whichever you choose, make sure hreflang tags are output correctly so search engines show the right version to the right country. Check them after setup rather than assuming.

steps.title: Show local currency
steps.text: Converted prices at minimum; shoppers should not do maths.

steps.title: Decide on rounding
steps.text: Prices like 23.47 look like a conversion. Rounding rules make them look intentional.

steps.title: Consider market-specific pricing
steps.text: Costs differ by region. Fixed local prices can protect margin.

steps.title: Be clear about duties and taxes
steps.text: Surprise charges at delivery are one of the worst international experiences.

blocks.text: Translation is more than product titles. Checkout, emails, size guides, policies, and error messages all need attention. Machine translation is a starting point, not the finish line: **have a native speaker review** your top pages and checkout before launch.

items: Translate shipping and returns policies for every market.
Localise size charts and units.
Check that theme text and app widgets are translated too.

blocks.text: Test each market as a real customer would: from that country (via VPN), on mobile, through to a completed order.

blocks.title: Market QA checklist
blocks.text: Check each of these per market before launch:
items: Currency on every page
Shipping rates
Tax display
Translated emails
Payment methods popular in that region

items: [Shopify SEO Technical Checklist](/shopify-technical-seo-checklist)
[Migrating to Shopify Plus](/migrating-to-shopify-plus)

items.q: Do I need Shopify Plus to sell internationally?
items.a: No. Markets features are available on standard plans, though some advanced options differ by plan. Check current plan details.

items.q: Should I translate my whole catalogue?
items.a: Start with bestsellers, navigation, checkout, and policies, then expand based on market performance.

items.q: Will international markets hurt my main SEO?
items.a: Not if hreflang and domain structure are set up correctly. Poor setup can cause duplicate content issues.

seo.title: QA for Discounts and Promotions: Stop Sale-Day Pricing Bugs | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Discount stacking, broken codes, and wrong prices cost money on your busiest days. A QA checklist for every promotion before it goes live.

hero.title: QA for Discounts and Promotions: Stop Sale-Day Pricing Bugs
hero.excerpt: Discount stacking, broken codes, and wrong prices cost money on your busiest days. A QA checklist for every promotion before it goes live.

intro.text: The most expensive bugs in e-commerce are not broken layouts. They are ==pricing bugs on sale day==: a code that stacks when it should not, a discount that applies to excluded products, or a banner promising 30% while checkout gives 20%. Each one either costs margin or costs trust, usually on the day with the most traffic.

blocks.text: Promotions touch many systems at once: discount rules, theme banners, product badges, apps, email campaigns, and ads. Each is set up by different people, often under deadline pressure. **The bugs live in the gaps between them.**

rows: Sale price not reverted after event

blocks.text: For each promotion, write down the rules in plain language, then test every combination that matters. A simple matrix keeps it systematic.

steps.title: Eligible product, single item
steps.text: Discount applies at the correct amount.

steps.title: Excluded product
steps.text: Discount does not apply, and the message is clear.

steps.title: Mixed cart
steps.text: Discount applies only to eligible items.

steps.title: Combined with other offers
steps.text: Stacking behaves exactly as intended.

steps.title: Edge thresholds
steps.text: Test just below and just above minimum spend.

blocks.text: Test with a real card to completion, then refund. Many discount bugs only appear at the final checkout step.

items: Announcement bar and homepage banners.
Product badges and strikethrough prices on collection and product pages.
Cart drawer and cart page totals.
Checkout and order confirmation email.
Landing pages linked from ads and email.

sections.heading: Plan the End as Carefully as the Start

blocks.text: Promotions fail at the end as often as the start. Schedule start and end times **in the right time zone**, confirm banners are scheduled to disappear, and do a quick post-event check that prices, badges, and codes have reverted.
Every promotion needs one person who signs off that it has been tested.

blocks.title: One name on the sign-off
blocks.text: Shared responsibility during a launch usually means nobody checked.

blocks.title: Related reading
blocks.text: Keep reading on the Ingversions blog:
items: [Building a Pre-Launch QA Process That Scales](/prelaunch-qa-process-that-scales)
[Automated UI Testing for E-commerce](/automated-ui-testing-ecommerce)

items.q: How early should promotions be set up?
items.a: At least a few days before launch, so there is time to test and fix without panic.

items.q: Can this be automated?
items.a: Parts of it. Automated checkout tests can verify cart totals for key scenarios, but a manual walk-through is still worth doing.

items.q: What should I do if a pricing bug goes live?
items.a: Pause the code or promotion first, then assess. Decide how to honour affected orders before customers ask.

seo.title: Using Claude to Mine Customer Reviews for CRO Insights | Ingversions Blog
seo.description: Your reviews contain your customers' real objections and deciding factors. Here is a repeatable workflow for turning them into test ideas with Claude.

hero.title: Using Claude to Mine Customer Reviews for CRO Insights
hero.excerpt: Your reviews contain your customers' real objections and deciding factors. Here is a repeatable workflow for turning them into test ideas with Claude.

intro.text: Your reviews are the largest body of customer research you own, and most stores only read the latest few. Buried in hundreds of reviews are the exact words customers use, the objections they had before buying, and the reasons they chose you. Claude can ==read all of them at once== and turn them into something your team can act on.

blocks.text: Export reviews from your review app as a spreadsheet. Include rating, date, product, and text. Add other voice-of-customer sources if you have them: post-purchase surveys, support tickets, and return reasons.

blocks.title: Strip personal data first
blocks.text: Remove names, emails, and order numbers before sharing data with any AI tool. You only need the words.
Asking 'what do customers think?' gets a vague answer. Ask specific questions that map to decisions on your site.

steps.title: Deciding factors
steps.text: What reasons do customers give for choosing this product?

steps.title: Pre-purchase doubts
steps.text: What were customers worried about before buying, and were those worries resolved?

steps.title: Disappointments
steps.text: What complaints come up repeatedly in 1 to 3 star reviews?

steps.title: Customer language
steps.text: Which exact words and phrases do customers use to describe the benefit?

blocks.text: Ask Claude to quote the reviews that support each theme and count how often it appears, so you can check its work against the source.

rows: Size guide higher on product page; fit notes
Show delivery estimate near the buy button
Use the customer's phrase in product copy

blocks.text: Each row becomes a hypothesis in your testing backlog, backed by real customer evidence.

With Claude connected to your data sources through **MCP**, this can become a recurring workflow: pull new reviews, compare themes with last month, and flag anything new. Trends matter more than a single snapshot.

items: Compare themes by product to find product-specific problems.
Track whether complaints fall after a site or product change.
Share a one-page summary with product, CX, and marketing.

sections.heading: Keep a Human in the Loop

blocks.text: AI summaries are a starting point.

blocks.title: Verify before you ship
blocks.text: Read a sample of the source reviews behind each major theme before acting on it, especially for anything that affects product claims or policies.

items.a: Patterns become useful from roughly a hundred reviews per product line, but even smaller sets surface clear objections.

items.q: Can Claude read reviews directly from my store?
items.a: With the right MCP connection or an export, yes. See our [MCP setup guide](/connect-claude-to-shopify-store-mcp-guide) for the options.

items.q: Is this better than a survey?
items.a: It complements one. Reviews show what customers say unprompted; surveys answer the questions you choose.
